title: A friend gives the hard thing
hookLine: seven marks of a friend: gives what is hard to give, does what is hard to do, bears what is hard to bear

lines: NOT ALWAYS WHO WE SEE MOST.
cards: Three in the morning, and the phone rings. Who would you call back? Who would call you?

Not the people who like your posts; the ones who'd pick up. That list is often short, and it doesn't always match the people we see the most. The Book of Sevens has a short sutta that tries to put that list into words.
It's addressed to the monks, but nothing in it is monastic: seven marks of a friend worth keeping close.

teach.b: A friend with seven qualities, the Buddha says, is worth associating with. One: they give what is hard to give. Two: they do what is hard to do.
Three: they bear what is hard to bear.
Four: they tell you their secrets. Five: they keep your secrets.
Six: they don't abandon you in misfortune. Seven: they don't look down on you when you're ruined. Look at the first three.
Anyone can give what's easy: a like, a quick text, the thing they didn't need anyway.

teach.h: A FRIEND GIVES THE HARD THING.
teach.b: A friend gives what costs something. Their Saturday. Their honesty, when it's awkward.
The patience to sit through your bad month. Four and five are a pair: trust going both ways. They let you in, and they don't let your life out.
Six and seven: the friend who stays when things fall apart, and who doesn't treat you differently when you've lost. That last one is sharp; it's easy to stay close to someone doing well.
The sutta ends in verse, repeating the seven, and says that whoever wants a friend should seek out a person like this. Two days ago, the six ways to be dear described what makes a community hold.
This is the same thing at the size of two people, and it can be read both ways at once: a list of friends to look for, and a list of how to be one.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes pair this sutta with the Buddha's teaching on good friendship, kalyanamittata, and lay Buddhists may read it as advice both for choosing friends and for being one.

o: anyone you see often and get along with
a teacher who guides your meditation
a friend who stays when things get hard

games.q: a friend gives the hard thing: tap the pairs.
p: hard to give, do and bear
doesn't look down when you're ruined

s: the sutta's friend keeps your secrets but never shares their own
it goes both ways: they tell you their secrets, and they keep yours.
not looking down on you when you're ruined is one of the seven marks
it's the seventh, right after not abandoning you in misfortune.
this sutta is only about friendships between monks
it's addressed to monks, but nothing in the seven marks is monastic.

games.q: you have two friends. one sends a quick text every day. one shows up once, on the worst night of your year. by the sutta's marks, which is the friend?
o: the one who showed up when it was hard.
games.why: the sutta's friend gives what's hard to give and doesn't abandon you in misfortune. it's not about how often, but about what it costs.

practice: Bring to mind a friend who once gave you something hard, time, honesty, patience, presence when things were bad, and let yourself feel grateful for a few breaths.
Then turn it around: picture a friend who might need something hard from you right now, and which of the seven you could be for them. Rest with that one.

wordCard.voice: mitta. The Pali word for friend, root of metta, behind the seven marks in the Book of Sevens: a true friend gives, does and bears what's hard, shares secrets, and stays through misfortune and ruin. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali mitta: friend; the word behind metta, the goodwill met on day 672.

carryVoice: Your line: give something that costs you. Hard to give, hard to do, hard to bear: that's the mark. Day six hundred seventy-seven.
